paragraphs: He really had no time to lose. Even as he was saying good-bye to Lise, it had struck him that he would have to find some trick for catching his brother Dmitri, who was plainly keeping out of his way. It was getting late, nearly three o’clock. Alyosha’s whole heart was drawn to the monastery, to his dying saint, but the need to see Dmitri outweighed everything. With every hour he grew more sure that some great and unavoidable disaster was about to happen. What the disaster was, and what he would say to his brother when it came, he could probably not have said clearly. “Even if my benefactor has to die without me, at least I won’t have to blame myself all my life for this: that I might have saved something and didn’t, but walked past and hurried home. If I do what I mean to do, I will be following his great teaching.”

His plan was to take his brother Dmitri by surprise. He would climb over the fence as he had the day before, get into the garden and sit in the summer-house. If Dmitri was not there, Alyosha thought, he would not announce himself to Foma or the women of the house. He would stay hidden in the summer-house, even if he had to wait there until evening. If Dmitri was lying in wait for Grushenka again, as before, he would very likely come to the summer-house. Alyosha did not think much about the details of his plan, however. He simply resolved to carry it out, even if it meant not getting back to the monastery that day.

Everything went off without a hitch. He climbed over the hurdle at almost the same spot as the day before and slipped into the summer-house unseen. He did not want to be noticed. The woman of the house, and Foma too if he was around, might be loyal to his brother and follow his orders. They might refuse to let Alyosha into the garden, or they might warn Dmitri that someone was looking for him and asking questions.

There was no one in the summer-house. Alyosha sat down and began to wait. He looked around the summer-house, which somehow struck him as a good deal older than before. The day was just as fine as yesterday, but this time the place looked wretched. There was a ring on the table, no doubt left by the glass of brandy that had been spilled the day before. Foolish, pointless ideas wandered through his mind, as they always do in a time of dull waiting. He wondered, for instance, why he had sat down in exactly the same place as before and not on the other seat. At last he felt very low, worn down by suspense and uncertainty. But he had not been sitting there even a quarter of an hour when he suddenly heard the twang of a guitar somewhere very close. Some people were sitting, or had only just sat down, in the bushes not more than twenty paces away. Alyosha suddenly remembered that on leaving the summer-house the day before he had caught sight of an old, low, green garden-seat among the bushes on the left, by the fence. The people must be sitting on it now. Who were they?
A man’s voice suddenly began to sing in a sugary falsetto, accompanying himself on the guitar:
I am bound to my dear by a force I cannot resist. O Lord, have mercy on her and on me! On her and on me! On her and on me!
The voice stopped. It was a servant’s tenor and a servant’s song. Then another voice, a woman’s, asked in a coaxing, shy tone, though with a mincing affectation:
“Why haven’t you been to see us for so long, Pavel Fyodorovitch? Why do you always look down on us?”

“Not at all,” answered a man’s voice, politely but with firm dignity. It was clear that the man held the upper hand and that the woman was making advances. “I think the man must be Smerdyakov,” thought Alyosha, “going by his voice. And the lady must be the daughter of the house, who has come from Moscow, the one who wears a dress with a train and goes to Marfa for soup.”
“I’m awfully fond of verses of all kinds, as long as they rhyme,” the woman’s voice went on. “Why don’t you go on?”
The man sang again:
What do I care for royal wealth If only my dear one is in health? Lord, have mercy On her and on me! On her and on me! On her and on me!
“It was even better last time,” remarked the woman’s voice. “You sang ‘If my darling is in health,’ and it sounded more tender. I suppose you’ve forgotten it today.”
“Poetry is rubbish!” said Smerdyakov curtly.
“Oh, no! I’m very fond of poetry.”

“As far as it is poetry, it is rubbish through and through. Think about it yourself: who ever talks in rhyme? And if we were all made to talk in rhyme, even by government decree, we wouldn’t get much said, would we? Poetry is no good, Marya Kondratyevna.”
“How clever you are! How is it you’ve gone so deep into everything?” The woman’s voice grew more and more coaxing.

“I could have done better than this. I could have known more than this, if it hadn’t been for my fate from childhood on. I would have shot a man in a duel if he called me names because I come from a filthy beggar and have no father. And they used to throw that in my face in Moscow. It had reached them from here, thanks to Grigory Vassilyevitch. Grigory Vassilyevitch blames me for rebelling against my birth, but I would have agreed to their killing me before I was born, so that I would never have come into the world at all. They used to say in the market, and your mamma too, with a great lack of delicacy, started telling me that her hair was like a mat on her head and that she was short of five foot by a wee bit. Why say a wee bit when she could have said ‘a little bit,’ like everyone else? She wanted to make it touching, a real peasant’s feeling. Can a Russian peasant be said to feel, compared with an educated man? In his ignorance he can’t be said to have any feeling at all. From childhood, whenever I hear ‘a wee bit,’ I’m ready to burst with rage. I hate all Russia, Marya Kondratyevna.”
“If you’d been a cadet in the army, or a young hussar, you wouldn’t talk like that. You would have drawn your saber to defend all Russia.”
“I don’t want to be a hussar, Marya Kondratyevna, and what’s more, I’d like to abolish all soldiers.”
“And when an enemy comes, who’s going to defend us?”

“There’s no need for defense. In 1812 there was a great invasion of Russia by Napoleon, first Emperor of the French, the father of the present one. It would have been a good thing if they had conquered us. A clever nation would have conquered a very stupid one and annexed it. We would have had quite different institutions.”

“Are things so much better in their country than in ours? I wouldn’t swap a dandy I know for three young Englishmen,” said Marya Kondratyevna tenderly, no doubt giving him a most languishing glance as she spoke.
“That depends on one’s taste.”
“But you’re just like a foreigner—just like a most gentlemanly foreigner. I tell you so, though it makes me bashful.”

“If you want to know, the people over there and ours here are just alike in their vice. They’re all swindlers. Only over there the scoundrel wears polished boots, and here he grovels in filth and sees no harm in it. The Russian people need a thrashing, as Fyodor Pavlovitch said very truly yesterday, though he is mad, and so are all his children.”
“You said yourself you had such respect for Ivan Fyodorovitch.”

“But he called me a stinking lackey. He thinks I might be unruly. He’s mistaken there. If I had a certain sum in my pocket, I would have left here long ago. Dmitri Fyodorovitch is lower than any lackey in his behavior, in his mind and in his poverty. He doesn’t know how to do anything, and yet everyone respects him. I may be only a soup-maker, but with some luck I could open a café restaurant in Petrovka, in Moscow, because my cooking is something special, and in Moscow, except for the foreigners, no one’s cooking is anything special. Dmitri Fyodorovitch is a beggar, but if he challenged the son of the first count in the country, that count would fight him. Yet in what way is he better than I am? He’s ever so much stupider than I am. Look at the money he has wasted for no reason!”
“A duel must be lovely,” Marya Kondratyevna said suddenly.
“How so?”

“It must be so dreadful and so brave, especially when young officers with pistols in their hands pop at each other for the sake of some lady. A perfect picture! Ah, if only girls were allowed to watch, I’d give anything to see one!”
“It’s all very well when you’re the one firing at somebody, but when he’s firing straight into your mug, you must feel pretty silly. You’d be glad to run away, Marya Kondratyevna.”
“You don’t mean you would run away?” But Smerdyakov did not condescend to answer. After a moment of silence the guitar tinkled again, and he sang again in the same falsetto:
Whatever you may say, I will go far away. Life will be bright and gay In the city far away. I won’t grieve, I won’t grieve at all, I don’t intend to grieve at all.

Then something unexpected happened. Alyosha suddenly sneezed. They fell silent. Alyosha got up and walked toward them. He found Smerdyakov dressed up and wearing polished boots, his hair pomaded and perhaps curled. The guitar lay on the garden-seat. His companion was the daughter of the house, in a light-blue dress with a train two yards long. She was young and would not have been bad-looking, if her face had not been so round and so terribly freckled.
“Will my brother Dmitri be back soon?” asked Alyosha, as calmly as he could.
Smerdyakov got up slowly, and Marya Kondratyevna rose too.
“How am I to know about Dmitri Fyodorovitch? It’s not as if I were his keeper,” answered Smerdyakov, quietly, distinctly and superciliously.
“But I only asked whether you know?” Alyosha explained.
“I know nothing about where he is, and I don’t want to.”
“But my brother told me that you keep him informed of everything that goes on in the house, and that you promised to let him know when Agrafena Alexandrovna comes.”
Smerdyakov turned a slow, unmoved look on him.
“And how did you get in this time, since the gate was bolted an hour ago?” he asked, looking at Alyosha.
“I came in from the back-alley, over the fence, and went straight to the summer-house. I hope you’ll forgive me,” he added, turning to Marya Kondratyevna. “I was in a hurry to find my brother.”

“Ach, as if we could take it amiss from you!” drawled Marya Kondratyevna, flattered by Alyosha’s apology. “Dmitri Fyodorovitch often goes to the summer-house that way. We don’t even know he’s here, and there he is, sitting in the summer-house.”
“I’m very anxious to find him, or to learn from you where he is now. Believe me, it’s about something of great importance to him.”
“He never tells us,” lisped Marya Kondratyevna.

“Though I used to come here as a friend,” Smerdyakov began again, “Dmitri Fyodorovitch has pestered me mercilessly even here, with his endless questions about the master. ‘What news?’ he’ll ask. ‘What’s going on in there now? Who’s coming and going?’ And can’t I tell him something more? Twice already he’s threatened me with death.”
“With death?” Alyosha exclaimed in surprise.

“Do you suppose he’d think much of that, with his temper, which you had a chance to see for yourself yesterday? He says if I let Agrafena Alexandrovna in and she spends the night there, I’ll be the first to suffer for it. I’m terribly afraid of him, and if I weren’t even more afraid of doing it, I ought to inform the police. God only knows what he might not do!”
“His honor said to him the other day, ‘I’ll pound you in a mortar!’” added Marya Kondratyevna.
“Oh, if it’s pounding in a mortar, it may be only talk,” said Alyosha. “If I could meet him, I might speak to him about that too.”

“Well, the only thing I can tell you is this,” said Smerdyakov, as though thinking better of it. “I’m here as an old friend and neighbor, and it would be odd if I didn’t come. On the other hand, Ivan Fyodorovitch sent me first thing this morning to your brother’s lodging in Lake Street, without a letter, but with a message for Dmitri Fyodorovitch to come and dine with him at the restaurant here, in the market-place. I went, but I didn’t find Dmitri Fyodorovitch at home, though it was eight o’clock. ‘He’s been here, but he’s quite gone,’ those were the very words of his landlady. It’s as though there were an understanding between them. Perhaps at this moment he’s in the restaurant with Ivan Fyodorovitch, because Ivan Fyodorovitch hasn’t been home to dinner, and Fyodor Pavlovitch dined alone an hour ago and has gone to lie down. But I most particularly ask you not to mention me or what I’ve told you, because he’d kill me for nothing at all.”
“Brother Ivan invited Dmitri to the restaurant today?” Alyosha repeated quickly.
“That’s so.”
“The Metropolis tavern in the market-place?”
“The very same.”
“That’s quite likely,” cried Alyosha, very excited. “Thank you, Smerdyakov; that’s important. I’ll go there at once.”
“Don’t betray me,” Smerdyakov called after him.
“Oh, no, I’ll go to the tavern as if by chance. Don’t worry.”
“But wait a minute, I’ll open the gate for you,” cried Marya Kondratyevna.
“No, it’s a short cut. I’ll get over the fence again.”

What he had heard threw Alyosha into great agitation. He ran to the tavern. He could not go into the tavern in his monastic dress, but he could ask at the entrance for his brothers and call them down. Just as he reached the tavern, though, a window was flung open, and his brother Ivan called down to him from it.
“Alyosha, can’t you come up here to me? I’d be awfully grateful.”
“Of course I can, only I’m not sure whether in this dress—”
“But I’m in a room apart. Come up the steps; I’ll run down to meet you.”
A minute later Alyosha was sitting beside his brother. Ivan was dining alone.
